name: Bianca Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take first calls on car insurance claims, so the call you make after a crash or when your car gets stolen. We're in a contact centre on an industrial estate, two buses from my flat. I take the details, calm people down, book the tow truck and the hire car. I like it when someone's shaking and by the end of the call they're laughing a bit. What wears me out is the system, which changes every year and logs me out if I'm slow.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Have they brought in any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They've got a thing that listens to the call and fills in the claim form, and they want us to check it instead of typing. I don't use it, I type it myself, because the one time I tried it put the wrong car registration on a claim and I got the blame. My partner Marco says I'm stubborn, and he's right, but I've been here six years doing it my way. We rent a small flat and between us we have about two weeks of money put aside, so I can't afford a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, people want a person when they've had a crash. Nobody rings a car insurer on a good day, so the least we can do is have a real person pick up the phone. Online I don't really post, but I'd tell my sister I was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be worried, just not about AI. The company's been talking about merging our site with another one two hours away, and if that happens I'm not going. And our rent went up again in September, so we're already counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and keep my call times good, because that's what keeps you off the list. I'd look for overtime on weekends, because the claims spike after storms and they pay time and a half. I'd probably start using the form tool a bit if my manager insisted, but only for the easy bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, honestly. Not frightened, just that low hum of knowing you're one change away from trouble. It's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is that what you'd normally do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your head down. Is that what you'd normally do?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the site merger happened, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'm not someone who makes noise. My mother always said do your job well and they'll keep you, and mostly that's been true. But I've also seen good people let go when a site closes, so I know it's not a guarantee.

say: I'd say **people want a person** when they've had a crash.
I'd tell my sister I was **right** about AI being hype.
think: A planned **site merger** worries her more than AI.
The **September rent rise** already has them counting every bill.
do: Keep **call times** good to stay off the redundancy list.
Take **storm overtime** at time and a half.
Use the form tool only for **easy bits** if pushed.
feel: A low **hum of worry**, one change away from trouble.
S0.quote: Nobody rings a car insurer on a good day, so the least we can do is have a real person pick up the phone.
fieldNote: Her worries come from a **site merger** and rent, not AI itself.
She avoids the AI form tool after it caused a **blamed mistake**.
Her partner's **bus depot** ties them to the town.

steps.text: Keep call times on target to stay off any redundancy list
Take weekend storm-claim overtime at time and a half

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company should keep the claims line human, because people don't trust a bot with a crash. I'd say it in team meetings, politely. I'm not a protest person, so I wouldn't go further than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be one of the first to go, because I'm the one who won't use the tools. They'll keep the people who can check what the AI does fastest, and that's not me. I'm not against computers, I'm against learning a new system every six months when the old one worked fine and I was good at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the form tool, because I'd have no choice, and I'd try to get quicker at checking it. I'd ask my aunt properly about the bakery, whether she needs someone full-time. I'd cut our streaming and stop going out on Saturdays, and try to keep a bit back in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in my stomach, and a bit embarrassed. I've always been good at my job, and suddenly being good isn't enough. I'd feel like I'd missed a bus everyone else saw coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who would you talk to first about it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd use the tool after all. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco, at night, after his late shift. He'd tell me not to worry, because that's what he does, and then he'd lie awake. Then my mother, who'd tell me to work harder, which doesn't help.

I'd say it **politely** in team meetings, not at protests.

S1.quote: I'm not against computers, I'm against learning a new system every six months when the old one worked fine and I was good at it.
fieldNote: She'd adopt AI only under **direct threat**, without pretending to like it.

Her **identity** as a good agent takes a hard knock.

steps.text: Start using the AI claim form tool and practise checking it
Ask her aunt about a full-time job at the bakery
Cancel streaming services and Saturday nights out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't know what to say, honestly. I'd probably say it's too fast and the government should slow it down. I wouldn't post anything, I'd just talk to Marco.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job is gone in the first year. Taking claims is all talking and typing, no hands. Two years means I'd be twenty-nine with no job, a boyfriend driving a bus, and a landlord who doesn't care about any of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to my aunt and ask for any hours at the bakery, and I'd take them. I'd cancel everything that isn't rent and food. I'd sign up for whatever government help appears, and if we couldn't make rent, we'd ask Marco's parents if we could stay with them for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone. I don't have a plan, and I don't have money to make one. I'd be frozen, and I hate being frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Marco's job, driving the bus?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What about Marco's job, driving the bus?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving's hands-on, so maybe 2031 on this card, but the buses already have those lane-assist things, so I don't know. Even three years of his wage would be something. But on his wage alone we can't pay rent, not here.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and the government should slow it.
I'd **talk to Marco** rather than post anything.
think: Her claims job is **gone** in the first year.
Taking claims is **all talking and typing**, with no hands-on cover.
do: Ask her aunt for **any bakery hours**.
Apply for **government help** and ask Marco's parents for a room.
feel: **Frozen**, with no plan and no money.
S2.quote: Two years means I'd be twenty-nine with no job, a boyfriend driving a bus, and a landlord who doesn't care about any of it.
fieldNote: She has **no plan** and no money to make one.
Her partner's driving job buys **about three years**, if that.
Her mother's belief that **hard work** protects you is shaken.

steps.text: Ask her aunt for any hours at the bakery counter
Cancel every bill except rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't much, and companies should be honest about which jobs are going. I'd say that at work, carefully. I still wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job would still go, just in 2031. If I've got five years, I'll probably spend four of them pretending it isn't coming, and I know that about myself. Marco would have to push me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools at work, because I'd have to, and try to stay in the job as long as possible. In the second or third year I'd do a food hygiene course and start some weekend shifts at the bakery, so I've got something hands-on. We'd try to save a bit, maybe thirty a month, which isn't much but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not frozen like the fast one. It's a slow knot rather than a punch. I'd still feel like I'm behind everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would Marco have to push you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Why would Marco have to push you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the bakery a real plan or a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I always wait. I waited three years to move out of my mother's, and two years to learn to drive, and I still haven't passed. I like things the way they are, and that's fine until it isn't.

say: I'd say companies must be **honest** about which jobs go.
I'd say it **carefully** at work and not post online.
think: Her claims job still goes, just later, in **2031**.
She'd likely **pretend** for four years that it isn't coming.
do: Use the **AI tools** to keep the job as long as possible.
Take a **food hygiene course** and weekend bakery shifts.
feel: A **slow knot** of worry rather than a punch.
S3.quote: If I've got five years, I'll probably spend four of them pretending it isn't coming, and I know that about myself.
fieldNote: She knows she **always waits** and needs her partner Marco to push.
The bakery is a **fallback**, not a passion.
She still expects to **lose her job**, only later.

steps.text: Use the AI claim tools to stay employed as long as possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is fair warning, and people should get help to retrain. At work I'd say it's far off. With friends I'd probably make a joke about being a bakery queen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd probably drift. Ten years is long enough for me to end up somewhere else by accident, which is how I ended up in insurance. I'd lose this job at thirty-seven, but I might have found something by then without really trying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job and use the tools when they tell me to. I'd do weekend shifts at the bakery, slowly, maybe learn the business side if my aunt wants to retire. And I'd try to finally pass my driving test, because that opens up jobs outside town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, honestly. It's still a worry, but it's a distant one, like a pension. I'd think about it on bad days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you take it seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you take it seriously?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing people on my floor actually lose their jobs. Until I see it, it's a story. Once Sandra on the next desk goes, I'd move.

say: I'd call **ten years** fair warning and want retraining help.
I'd **joke** with friends about becoming a bakery queen.
think: She'd probably **drift** into something else by accident, as before.
She still expects to **lose this job** at thirty-seven.
do: Keep the job and use **AI tools** when told.

feel: **Calmer**, a distant worry like a pension.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to end up somewhere else by accident, which is how I ended up in insurance.
fieldNote: She'd only act once **colleagues actually lose** their jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have no time and no money and no plan. What would help is somebody telling me, clearly, what jobs will still exist, and paying me to learn one. I don't need a lecture, I need a list.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the customers lose. I've cried with people whose car just got written off, and I'd like to see a computer do that and mean it. That's what the job actually is, and nobody counts it.

headlineQuote: I've cried with people whose car just got written off, and I'd like to see a computer do that and mean it.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old** car insurance claims agent who never uses AI tools.
She rents with her partner Marco, a bus driver, and they have about **two weeks** saved.
She is **pragmatic**, quiet and prefers to keep her head down rather than protest.
Her fallback in every scenario is her aunt's **bakery**, which she sees as second best.
She moves from **anxious** to panicked, easing only with ten years' warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time, money or plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear list** of jobs that will still exist.
**Paid training** to learn one of them.
